The Red-knobbed imperial pigeon is a large, frugivorous columbid endemic to the Bismarck Archipelago and Solomon Islands. Adult females attain a substantial body size, with a maximum recorded wet weight in the wild of 652 grams [Wwi = 652 grams], a figure derived from a series of field-measured specimens where the range spanned 628 to 722 grams. Hatchlings emerge from the egg at a much smaller scale, with a neonatal wet weight of 29.7 grams [Ww0 = 29.7 grams], a value estimated from the closely related congener Ducula pistrinaria due to limited data directly from this species. This initial mass is somewhat modest for a pigeon of this ultimate size, suggesting a relatively protracted period of parental provisioning during the early nestling phase. The eggs themselves are incubated at approximately 39 °C [T = 39 °C], a thermal environment that yields a short incubation period; field observations confirm that hatching occurs after an average of 27 days [ab = 27 days] of constant brooding by both parents.

Continuing the theme of thermally dependent development, the nestling period is also closely tied to the ambient temperatures typical of the lowland rainforest habitat. Under the warm, stable conditions of the breeding season (commonly averaging 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]), chicks achieve fledging after exactly 27 days since birth [tx = 27 days since birth]. This rapid transition from hatchling to independence reflects the high metabolic demands of a rapidly growing altricial chick. The basal metabolic rate of this species, measured via respirometry under such thermoneutral conditions, was recorded at 245.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 245.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that represents the maximum resting oxygen consumption for a non-growing, post-absorptive adult at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This metabolic rate is consistent with predictions for a large-bodied fruit pigeon and underscores the energetic intensity required to sustain such a fast developmental schedule.

The onset of reproductive capability in the Red-knobbed imperial pigeon is delayed until well after the fledging stage, following an extended subadult period. Under the same thermal conditions of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], individuals do not reach puberty until approximately 81 days since birth [tp = approximately 81 days since birth]. This period of sexual maturation likely corresponds to the time required for full skeletal and muscular development, as well as the acquisition of foraging skills necessary to support the energetic costs of reproduction. The attainment of puberty marks a critical transition, but actual breeding is often deferred even further. The first successful reproductive event, or age at first brood, occurs considerably later, at roughly 985 days since birth [tR = roughly 985 days since birth], a value equivalent to about 2.7 year at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]s of age. This prolonged delay between physiological maturity and first breeding is typical of large, long-lived columbids and is likely shaped by the need to secure a high-quality territory.

The species' life-history strategy is one of slow replacement, characterized by a modest annual reproductive output and an exceptionally long life span. In terms of fecundity, females produce a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], with only one such clutch laid per year [F_R_i = one such clutch laid per year]. This extremely low annual reproductive rate is among the most conservative of any pigeon species and is balanced by a remarkably high adult survival rate. Maximum longevity in the wild has been estimated at approximately 6169 days [am = approximately 6169 days], or nearly 17 years, based on field recapture records and mark-resighting studies conducted under ambient thermal conditions averaging 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. Such an extended life span is adaptive in an environment where juvenile mortality is high, allowing adults multiple breeding seasons in which to contribute offspring to the population.

An extended life span of nearly 6169 days [am = nearly 6169 days] permits a protracted reproductive window, which is critically important given an annual fecundity of just 1 egg p at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]er year. This extreme iteroparity, where a single female might produce only 15 to 20 eggs over her entire lifetime, places a premium on parental investment and nest-site fidelity. The metabolic machinery supporting this long life is reflected in the measured basal oxygen consumption of 245.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 245.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a rate that remains consistent across repeated field trials at a thermoneutral temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C].
